Empirical Research Plan: “Public-school Quality, Private-school Supply and Housing Prices in Paris, 1997-2004”

-------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------------
Method: Geographic Regression-Discontinuity Design (often called a “boundary discontinuity” design).

Justification  
•  Assignment to each public middle school changes discretely at legally-defined catchment borders, while housing, streets and other local amenities vary smoothly in space.  
•  Flat-level geocodes (Lambert II) let us locate every sale relative to the nearest boundary with meter precision.  
•  Boundaries were fixed throughout 1997-2004 and are historically unrelated to the spatial distribution of private schools, which has been stable for decades because entry is tightly regulated.  
•  A spatial RDD therefore allows us to compare prices of otherwise similar dwellings located very near—but on opposite sides of—the same boundary.  
•  To study how private-school supply moderates the price premium, we interact the treatment indicator with an exogenous measure of private-school availability (number of private collèges within 1 km).  This gives a “difference-in-discontinuities” (a.k.a. triple-difference) estimate.

-------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------------
•  Running variable: signed distance (in meters) from the dwelling to the nearest catchment boundary segment; distances < 0 belong to the lower-performing side, distances > 0 to the higher-performing side.  

•  Cut-off: distance = 0 (the legal boundary).  

•  Treatment indicator (T_i): 1 if the flat lies on the side served by the higher-performing public school among the two schools that share the focal boundary segment; 0 otherwise.  
   – Performance measured by the within-period average Brevet score (main spec.).  
   – Normalise school quality to mean 0, sd 1 city-wide so coefficients can be read as “per-sd quality”.  

•  Control group: flats on the lower-quality side inside a narrow symmetric bandwidth h around the boundary (e.g., 0–200 m).  

•  Moderator: PrivateSupply_i = number of private collèges inside a 1 km circle around the dwelling (or indicator ≥1).  

•  Time dimension: Transactions 1997-2004 with year fixed effects; the location of boundaries and private schools is time-invariant, public-school performance varies slowly, so identification comes almost entirely from the cross-sectional boundary contrast.

-------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------------
A1. Local continuity of potential outcomes. Conditional on distance-to-boundary (and boundary-segment fixed effects), housing prices and unobservable amenities evolve smoothly in space; only the assigned public school quality jumps.  
– Plausible: Boundaries are idiosyncratic zig-zags; they rarely coincide with arrondissement or census-block borders.

A2. No precise sorting on either side of the boundary within the small bandwidth.  
– Plausible: Flats are long-lived assets; sellers cannot move buildings across the street. Families can choose which side to buy on, but within 100–200 m choices are constrained by availability and price, and manipulation would show up as discontinuities in observables (testable).

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA). The presence of a high-quality neighbour school does not itself affect prices except through assignment.  
– Reasonable at the micro scale we are using; spillovers decay quickly with distance.

A4. Private-school supply is predetermined and exogenous to 1997-2004 boundary quality differentials.  
– Plausible: Openings are tightly regulated, and nearly all private schools pre-date the sample period.

-------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
-------------------------------------------------------
T1. Boundaries may coincide with unobserved amenity changes (e.g., a park, a metro stop).  
  Remedy: Boundary-segment fixed effects (one FE per contiguous segment) soak up any jump that is constant across the segment. Covariate balance tests (building age, floor, rooms, census income) further check smoothness.

T2. Differential sorting of higher-income families just inside the high-quality side.  
  Remedy: (i) Show no discontinuity in buyer income proxies (e.g., room/area ratio, notary-reported socio-professional category).  
  (ii) “Donut RD” excluding flats within 0–30 m of the border where selection could be strongest.  
  (iii)  Use census-block fixed effects interacted with distance polynomial as robustness.

T3. Measurement error in geocodes or mis-matched year-specific exam data.  
  Remedy: Keep only observations with geocoding precision ≤ 20 m; use three different performance measures (test scores, high-school track entry, socio-economic composition) and show consistent results.

-------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################################
# 0. Packages
############################################################
library(data.table)
library(sf)          # spatial operations
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects regressions
library(rdrobust)    # RD inference

############################################################
# 1. Load and merge data
############################################################
prop  <- fread("bien_transactions.csv")          # 200k rows
schools_pub <- fread("public_schools.csv")       # with quality
schools_priv <- fread("private_schools.csv")     # coordinates
borders <- st_read("catchment_boundaries.shp")   # polygons

# Convert to sf
prop_sf  <- st_as_sf(prop, coords = c("x_lambert","y_lambert"), crs = 2154) # Lambert II

############################################################
# 2. Construct running variable and treatment
############################################################
# a. Find nearest boundary segment and signed distance
#    Positive if school_quality(boundary_side)==high
#    We first rasterise: each polygon gets its school id; take boundary between polygons
borders_line <- st_boundary(st_union(borders))        # boundary lines
# Compute distance and side (sign)
prop_sf$dist <- st_distance(prop_sf, borders_line, by_element = TRUE)
# We also need which polygon contains the point
prop_sf$school_id <- st_within(prop_sf, borders) |> as.integer()
# Merge school quality
prop_sf <- merge(prop_sf, schools_pub, by="school_id")

# b. For each boundary, identify the two adjacent schools and mark high vs low
# Create key with boundary id, two schools and their quality difference
# *** For brevity, we assume we have computed:
#     prop_sf$boundary_id  and prop_sf$high_side (1/0)
#     prop_sf$dist_signed  (positive on high-quality side)

############################################################
# 3. Private-school availability
############################################################
priv_sf <- st_as_sf(schools_priv, coords = c("x","y"), crs = 2154)
# Count private schools within 1 km
prop_sf$priv1km <- lengths(st_is_within_distance(prop_sf, priv_sf, dist = 1000))
prop_sf$priv_dummy <- (prop_sf$priv1km>0)*1

############################################################
# 4. Keep observations within chosen bandwidth (±200 m)
############################################################
band <- 200
sample <- prop_sf[abs(prop_sf$dist_signed) <= band, ]

############################################################
# 5. Main specification: boundary fixed effects, side indicator,
#    interaction with private-school supply
############################################################
sample$log_price_m2 <- log(sample$price / sample$size_m2)

est <- feols(log_price_m2 ~ high_side*priv_dummy + poly(dist_signed, 1, raw = TRUE) | 
             boundary_id + year, data = sample,
             cluster = ~boundary_id)

summary(est)

############################################################
# 6. Robustness: different bandwidth (100 m) & donut RD (omit 0–30 m)
############################################################
sample_rb <- prop_sf[abs(prop_sf$dist_signed) <= 100 & abs(prop_sf$dist_signed) > 30,]
est_rb <- feols(log_price_m2 ~ high_side*priv_dummy + poly(dist_signed,1) |
                boundary_id + year, data = sample_rb, cluster=~boundary_id)
summary(est_rb)

############################################################
# 7. Covariate balance check (placebo)
############################################################
feols(size_m2 ~ high_side | boundary_id, data = sample) |> summary()
```

-------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: Families value peer quality highly when their child must attend the assigned public school. Where affordable private alternatives exist nearby, willingness to pay for residence-based access should fall.

•  Main effect (β₁): Flats on the higher-quality side but in areas with no nearby private school should sell for roughly 4 – 6 % more per square-meter per one-standard-deviation increase in public-school performance (based on prior European hedonic estimates of 2–10 %).  

•  Interaction (β₂): In zones with at least one private collège inside 1 km, that premium should shrink by perhaps one-half, i.e., an attenuation of 2–3 p.p.

-------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Spatial RDD)
-------------------------------------------------------
C1: No manipulation of running variable (distance) ………………… 0.8  
C2: Covariates smooth at cutoff (verified empirically) ……………… 0.8  
C3: Functional-form & bandwidth correctly chosen (tested) ………… 0.7  
C4: Single treatment jump; no other policies at border ……………… 0.7  
C5: Sufficient observations near cutoff for power …………………… 1.0  
Overall average ≈ 0.8 ⇒ method judged credible with standard robustness checks.

-------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
